issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategies imply a current external danger/assault-style threat context (arming oneself, hypervigilant scanning for physical threat) that is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness, where danger is usually medical and not mitigated by carrying a weapon or scanning for attackers.

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: Within the profile, these threat-focused safety behaviours are not supported by any Threat items and fit poorly with the formulation, which has Triggers and Threat fully inactive; they suggest a strong trigger/threat loop that the rest of the self-report does not reflect.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: The contamination appraisal is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of a child's life-threatening illness. It is more characteristic of interpersonal/sexual trauma or moral injury and lacks support from the other selected items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: Avoiding medical cues is plausible for a child's severe illness, but the additional strategies of avoiding public transport and constantly scanning for external threat suggest a danger-based trauma context not represented in the memory or appraisal items.

issues.item: Avoid Public Transport: Using public transport
issues.explanation: For trauma centered on a child's life-threatening illness, avoiding public transport is hard to link clinically unless other items indicate transport-related reminders or hospital-travel cues; no such trigger or memory content is present here, so this strategy appears context-mismatched.

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: Constantly scanning the environment for threat implies an ongoing external danger focus, but the rest of the profile is dominated by trauma-memory disorganisation and self-change appraisals rather than current external-threat concerns. With Threat and Trigger links inactive, this item sits awkwardly in the formulation.

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: This item is hard to reconcile with the trauma type (child's life-threatening illness) and the rest of the profile. The selected appraisals and memory items center on traumatic recollection, permanent change, and distrust, but not on a current external danger context. 'Constantly scan environment for signs of threat' implies hypervigilance for immediate environmental threat, which is more characteristic of assault/combat-type trauma and is not clinically linked here given that all Triggers and Threat edges are inactive in the formulation. It also sits poorly with the other maladaptive strategies, which are illness/trauma-processing related (avoid care, suppress thoughts).

vignette: Mr. Tran, a 69-year-old South Eastern Asian widower and nanny, has been struggling with the aftermath of his grandson's life-threatening illness several years ago. This event, which occurred when Mr. Tran was taking care of his young grandson while the parents were away on business, left him feeling profoundly changed and unable to make sense of what happened. The night started like any other until a sudden high fever turned into severe convulsions that sent both of them rushing to the emergency room. The harrowing moments in the ER-seeing his grandson's body thrashing uncontrollably and then slipping into unconsciousness-felt more real than anything Mr. Tran had experienced before. Now, these memories feel like they are happening all over again, as if the trauma was a recent event rather than something that happened years ago. Mr. Tran has come to believe that his actions during this crisis were what kept his grandson alive, and yet he feels unrecognizable to himself-a person who once was calm and steady but is now plagued by an ever-present fear of making mistakes again. This belief has deepened his sense of distrust towards others; he feels people are not what they seem, and this fuels a constant vigilance that makes it difficult for him to relax. This heightened state of alertness manifests in how Mr. Tran interacts with the world around him. He tries hard not to think about the trauma but finds himself constantly seeking distractions, keeping his mind occupied all the time. When he does allow himself to think about what happened, those memories feel overwhelmingly vivid and real, as if they are happening again right now. This recurrent intensity makes it challenging for Mr. Tran to maintain a coherent story of the event; he cannot even tell a clear account of what happened to himself. Mr. Tran's fear that his experiences have permanently changed him for the worse has led him to avoid seeking medical or psychological help, as he believes there is no point in doing so. Instead, he relies on suppressing thoughts and distracting himself with other tasks. This avoidance, however, only deepens his negative appraisals. He finds it increasingly difficult to trust others and is convinced that any attempt to seek help will only remind him of the trauma. The intense memories also exacerbate his maladaptive strategies. Whenever Mr. Tran thinks about seeking medical care, the vividness of those traumatic moments immediately surfaces, making such actions seem impossible. This cycle leaves him feeling trapped in a perpetual state of fear and self-doubt. Mr. Tran's daily life as a nanny has become increasingly strained due to these challenges. He avoids taking on tasks that might trigger memories of his grandson's illness, leading to fewer hours at work and strained relationships with the families he cares for. Despite these consequences, Mr. Tran is reluctant to address his fears directly because he believes that doing so will only reinforce his belief in a permanently damaged self. What finally brought Mr. Tran to seek help was the realization that his grandson's illness had profoundly affected not just him but also those around him. He is most afraid of losing control again, of being unable to protect someone he loves. At the same time, he hopes for a way to find peace and regain some sense of who he used to be. Mr. Tran understands that addressing these fears will require facing them head-on, but he is determined to do so in order to reclaim his life and find a path forward.
